lesson.title: The -ION Bridge
lesson.subtitle: Thousands of nouns convert whole — and every one is feminine

hook.title: One Ending, a Whole Warehouse
hook.content: Whenever an English word ends in -ion — invitation, opinion, tradition, participation — you can identify it as Latin-dressed. And most Latin English came through French. So the word is probably the same in French: invitation, opinion, tradition. No conversion needed; the ending IS the bridge.

footnotes.title: How many?
footnotes.content: Thousands: nation, situation, opération, réaction, mission, question… If you can read this sentence, you can already read hundreds of French nouns.

pattern.title: la — the -ION Nouns Are All Feminine
pattern.content: The cake took le. The -ION nouns take la: la collection, la tradition, la confirmation. And that is a decode rule, not memory: -ION is on the feminine squad, along with -té and -ance (coming in lesson 6). When you refer back to one of them — it — French says la again: je la veux. The article you chose for 'the' is the pronoun you use for 'it'.

footnotes.title: The half-said N
footnotes.content: In collection, the final N is thought, not said: /kɔlɛksjɔ̃/. Move toward the N, then stop — that 'not arriving' nasalizes the whole vowel. You'll meet this sound everywhere; for now, just don't land on the N.

pattern.linguist_note: Latin -tiō → French -tion with the N nasalized. English borrowed the spelling and kept the N audible; French kept the spelling and silenced it — the most polite disagreement in the two languages.
pattern.trap_note: The tempting wrong move: le, because most things you've met so far took le. The -ION squad is feminine — la collection, l'opinion. The ending tells you.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the French feminine noun meaning 'viewpoint / belief' (opin + ion):
exercises.explanation: opin + ion = opinion. The spelling converts whole; only the sounds move (nasal O, half-said N).
opinion starts with a vowel, so la loses its a: l'opinion. The apostrophe marks the sacrifice.

exercises.prompt: Convert each English -ION noun to French — all with their article:
exercises.target_answer: la tradition, la confirmation, la réservation, l'organisation, la passion, la complication
exercises.explanation: Every -ION noun takes la — elided to l' before a vowel. One squad, one article, thousands of words.

exercises.idea: I want it — and the it is the confirmation
cues: The it borrows la confirmation's article → la
Walk it left: I it want
exercises.explanation: je la veux — the same left-walk, now with a feminine it. The article you chose for 'the' is the pronoun for 'it'.

diagnosis.cue: It wears the noun's article: la confirmation → je la veux. The -ION squad is feminine.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.explanation: Two -AN nasals in one sentence: tradition, importante. Think the N, don't say it.
exercises.affirmation: Both nasals landed — you thought the N twice and said it zero times.

twist.prompt: Ungraded, just to feel it — 'Do you want the invitation?'
twist.explanation: l'invitation — the elision fires again. Notice how the question needed no new machinery: just the voice.

payoff.text: Remember la, the feminine 'the' left waiting in lesson 1? Here is her payoff: the -ION engine made her the most loaded article in French — thousands of nouns, every one hers.

summary.outcome: Convert any -ION noun, mark it feminine with la (elided to l'), and refer to it with la after the left-walk.

use_example.german: Je veux la confirmation. — Je la veux.
use_example.english: I want the confirmation. — I want it.

summary.takeaway: -ION is a gender decoder: the ending is feminine, the article is la, and 'it' is that same la, walking.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on Le Pont ([201] L'Elision Gym): see how The -ION Bridge leads directly into L'Elision Gym.

foreshadow.line: Now that thousands of -ION nouns are in your pocket, what happens when you slice off -ation and bolt on -er?

collection.etymology_derivation: Latin collectio. The -ION ending is your passport: thousands of nouns cross unchanged — and every one is feminine.

tradition.etymology_derivation: Latin traditio 'a handing over' — a tradition is what gets handed over.

confirmation.etymology_derivation: The nasal N is thought, not said: confiRmation with the N half-swallowed.

organisation.etymology_derivation: English spells -ization, French -isation — one S, never a Z, in French.

opinion.etymology_derivation: Latin opinio 'what one supposes'. Starts with a vowel, so la loses its a: l'opinion.

réservation.etymology_derivation: English wrote the accent out; French kept the é so you know where the stress lands.

complication.etymology_derivation: Two nasals, one rule: con- and -tion both think their N without saying it.

passion.etymology_derivation: Latin passio 'suffering' — passion is what you suffer for.

invitation.etymology_derivation: in- + vitare; the invitation is the not-refusing.

la.etymology_derivation: ille's feminine illa → la. Before a vowel it loses its a: l'opinion.

ion.name: The -ION Bridge
ion.phonetic_rule: Spelling converts 1:1; the final N is nasalised — thought, not said (collection /kɔlɛksjɔ̃/).
ion.historical_linguistics: English absorbed thousands of Latin-dress nouns through Norman French and later Renaissance borrowing. The -tion/-sion endings are the single largest cognate landing zone between the two languages.
ion.philological_note: Every -ION noun is feminine, so the article is la — elided to l' before a vowel. The ending is a gender decoder, not a memory item.
ion.literature_source: Walter, Le français dans tous les sens (1988); Pope, From Latin to Modern French (1952).
